title: SUBTE Monitor — Buenos Aires Transit Live Tracking
text:
SUBTE Monitor — Buenos Aires Transit Live Tracking
**Entrega:** Proyecto Informático 13/07 · 2026

**URL en vivo:** [https://subte-monitor.vercel.app](https://subte-monitor.vercel.app)

---

Resumen
Sistema de monitoreo en tiempo real de la red de subterráneos de Buenos Aires. Consume la API oficial GTFS-RT del GCBA y visualiza la posición estimada de cada formación sobre un mapa interactivo, con predicciones de arribo, alertas de servicio, y un planificador de rutas.

---

title: Stack Tecnológico
text:
SUBTE Monitor — Buenos Aires Transit Live Tracking > Stack Tecnológico
| Capa | Tecnología |
|------|-----------|
| Frontend | Next.js 16 (Turbopack, App Router) · React 19 · Tailwind CSS v4 |
| Tiempo real | GTFS Realtime · Algoritmo de clustering DBSCAN 1D · IDs estables |
| Mapa | Leaflet.js con interpolación de posición sobre shapes GTFS |
| Backend | API Routes (Next.js) |
| Base de datos | PostgreSQL (Neon) · Prisma ORM |
| Deploy | Vercel (serverless) |

---

text:
SUBTE Monitor — Buenos Aires Transit Live Tracking > Funcionalidades

|----------|------------|
| **Mapa** | Leaflet con trenes en movimiento, coloreados por línea. Pin de seguimiento. |
| **Arribos** | Cuadro de próximos trenes filtrable por línea, con ETA en tiempo real. |
| **Estado** | Alertas oficiales del GCBA + reportes de usuarios. |
| **Estaciones** | Malla de estaciones con datos de accesibilidad y pasajeros. |
| **Planificador** | Rutas óptimas entre estaciones (Dijkstra), filtro step-free. |

SUBTE Monitor — Buenos Aires Transit Live Tracking > Funcionalidades > Adicional

- **Clustering**: Las predicciones por estación se agrupan en "trenes virtuales" usando proyección temporal + DBSCAN.

*   **Framework**: [Next.js 15+ (App Router)](file:///home/juan/Programación/subte-monitor/src/app) con renderizado híbrido. El punto de entrada inicial es del lado del servidor (SSR) para cargar los datos de estaciones estáticas desde la base de datos, y luego pasa el control al cliente para la telemetría en tiempo real. *   **Base de Datos y ORM**: **PostgreSQL** administrado a través de **Prisma ORM (v6)**. title: 3. Algoritmos Centrales y Lógica de Telemetría
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 3. Algoritmos Centrales y Lógica de Telemetría
El mayor desafío técnico del Subte de Buenos Aires es que la API oficial de tránsito **no provee un identificador único persistente para las formaciones físicas en circulación**. En su lugar, provee un mapa plano de arribos estimados por andén (ej. "el próximo tren a Catedral llegará a la estación Agüero en 180 segundos").

Para resolver esto sin base de datos en memoria o sesiones complejas, se implementaron dos algoritmos clave en [`src/lib/telemetry.ts`](file:///home/juan/Programación/subte-monitor/src/lib/telemetry.ts):

title: A. Algoritmo de Ranuras de Vía Fijas (Fixed Track-Slot)
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 3. Algoritmos Centrales y Lógica de Telemetría > A. Algoritmo de Ranuras de Vía Fijas (Fixed Track-Slot)
Este algoritmo agrupa los arribos estimados en el espacio-tiempo. 1. Para cada línea y dirección, se leen todas las predicciones de arribos. 2. Cada predicción indica que un tren llegará a la estación $S$ en el tiempo absoluto $T_{arribo} = T_{actual} + ETA$. 3. Se proyecta hacia atrás en el tiempo cuándo partió ese tren de la terminal de origen ($T_{inicio\_viaje}$), restándole el tiempo nominal acumulado de viaje desde la terminal hasta la estación $S$. 4. Se agrupan estas estimaciones de partida ($T_{inicio\_viaje}$) utilizando un algoritmo de **Clustering 1D (similar a DBSCAN 1D)**.

title: A. Algoritmo de Ranuras de Vía Fijas (Fixed Track-Slot)
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 3. Algoritmos Centrales y Lógica de Telemetría > A. Algoritmo de Ranuras de Vía Fijas (Fixed Track-Slot)
Si dos predicciones de andén distintas apuntan a un tiempo de inicio de viaje con una diferencia menor a 3 minutos, se asume que se refieren a **la misma formación física**. 5. Las estimaciones agrupadas forman un "tren aislado" virtual con sus respectivas paradas y horarios programados de arribo a lo largo de la línea.

title: B. Hashing Estable (Stable Hashing)
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 3. Algoritmos Centrales y Lógica de Telemetría > B. Hashing Estable (Stable Hashing)
Para asignar un identificador persistente (ej. `A-4EF2`) a cada grupo (tren virtual) de manera stateless (sin estado):
1. Se calcula el promedio de los tiempos proyectados de inicio de viaje ($T_{inicio\_viaje}$) de las predicciones del clúster. 2. Se redondea este tiempo en cubos de **150 segundos** ($T_{redondeado}$). Esto evita fluctuaciones leves de estimación en la API entre consultas consecutivas. 3. Se genera un hash MD5 combinando:
   $$\text{Hash} = \text{MD5}(\text{routeId} + \text{directionId} + T_{redondeado})$$
4. Se toman los primeros 4 caracteres hex del hash para componer el ID final: `[Línea]-[4-HEX-CHARS]`.

title: B. Hashing Estable (Stable Hashing)
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 3. Algoritmos Centrales y Lógica de Telemetría > B. Hashing Estable (Stable Hashing)
Este ID se mantendrá estable durante todo el recorrido del tren por la línea y cambiará únicamente cuando inicie una nueva vuelta (trip).

title: C. Holding at the Signal (Confirmación Estricta de Eventos)
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 3. Algoritmos Centrales y Lógica de Telemetría > C. Holding at the Signal (Confirmación Estricta de Eventos)
Esta arquitectura resuelve el problema de **teletransportación de formaciones** cuando la API del GCBA sufre latencia.

El problema: cuando la API se congela por N segundos, el reloj local (`nowUnix`) sigue avanzando. Las condiciones matemáticas del filtrado eliminaban estaciones del array y el tren "saltaba" a la siguiente sin confirmación real.

title: C. Holding at the Signal (Confirmación Estricta de Eventos)
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 3. Algoritmos Centrales y Lógica de Telemetría > C. Holding at the Signal (Confirmación Estricta de Eventos)
**Las 3 Reglas de Oro:**
1. **`etaEnPaquete`**: Cada parada almacena su ETA relativa al timestamp del paquete de la API (`arr.arrivalTime - feedTimestamp`). Si la API se congela, este valor se congela con ella.
2. **Selección inmutable del `activeStop`**: Se evalúa contra `etaEnPaquete >= -40` en vez de contra `nowUnix`. La estación objetivo solo cambia cuando la API envía un paquete confirmando que ya pasó.
3. **Techo de cristal en 0.95**: El reloj local solo se usa para interpolar el progreso visual, pero se limita a `Math.min(0.95, ...)`. Si el reloj llega al final del tramo pero la API no confirma, el tren se queda clavado al 95% ("esperando en la señal").

title: C. Holding at the Signal (Confirmación Estricta de Eventos)
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 3. Algoritmos Centrales y Lógica de Telemetría > C. Holding at the Signal (Confirmación Estricta de Eventos)
**Dead Reckoning**: Para trenes temporalmente ausentes del feed (hasta 40s), se fuerza `IN_TRANSIT` con techo 0.95. Nunca se confirma arribo a andén sin datos frescos.

---

title: 4. Visualización en Mapa e Interpolación Geoespacial
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 4. Visualización en Mapa e Interpolación Geoespacial
El mapa interactivo full-screen está renderizado en **Leaflet** de forma nativa en [`src/components/SubteDashboard.tsx`](file:///home/juan/Programación/subte-monitor/src/components/SubteDashboard.tsx).

title: 4. Visualización en Mapa e Interpolación Geoespacial
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 4. Visualización en Mapa e Interpolación Geoespacial
A. Capa de Mosaicos y Tema Oscuro
Para lograr una estética de centro de control premium y unificada con Stitch UI:
1. Se utiliza el proveedor de mosaicos estándar de **OpenStreetMap** (OSM).
2. Se inyecta una capa de filtros CSS personalizados sobre los elementos de imagen de Leaflet (`.leaflet-tile`) para invertir y cambiar el tono de las calles:
   ```css
   .leaflet-tile {
     filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg) brightness(0.9) contrast(1.15) grayscale(0.2) !important;
   }
   ```
3. Esto genera un mapa completamente oscuro con calles en gris claro y agua en tonos oscuros, sirviendo de contraste perfecto para los trazos brillantes de las líneas de subte.

title: B. Interpolación Geoespacial y Snapping
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 4. Visualización en Mapa e Interpolación Geoespacial > B. Interpolación Geoespacial y Snapping
Cuando un tren se encuentra `IN_TRANSIT` entre su estación anterior ($S_{prev}$) y su estación siguiente ($S_{next}$):
1. Se calcula el `progress` decay del trayecto:
   $$\text{progress} = \max\left(0.0, \min\left(0.95, 1 - \frac{\text{segundosParaArriboLocal}}{90}\right)\right)$$
2. En lugar de interpolar en línea recta entre las dos estaciones (lo que haría que el tren atraviese manzanas y edificios en diagonal), el motor de renderizado realiza **snapping geoespacial de alta resolución**:
   - Obtiene el shape oficial de la línea (un arreglo ordenado de puntos geográficos) cargado en `src/lib/shapes.ts`. - Busca el segmento de vía delimitado por las coordenadas geográficas de $S_{prev}$ y $S_{next}$.

title: B. Interpolación Geoespacial y Snapping
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 4. Visualización en Mapa e Interpolación Geoespacial > B. Interpolación Geoespacial y Snapping
- Interpola la posición exacta del tren a lo largo de este trazado curvo según el porcentaje de progreso calculado. Esto hace que el tren ruede con total precisión física sobre las curvas reales de la red ferroviaria subterránea.

title: 5. Sistema de Seguimiento Direccional y Pineo
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 5. Sistema de Seguimiento Direccional y Pineo
Las últimas mejoras introducidas mejoran radicalmente la experiencia de usuario resolviendo las necesidades de dirección, tracking y limpieza:

title: 5. Sistema de Seguimiento Direccional y Pineo
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 5. Sistema de Seguimiento Direccional y Pineo
A. Indicador de Rumbo del Tren (Heading Vector)
Para indicar hacia dónde se dirige el tren sin depender únicamente de la dirección binaria (Id 0 o 1):
1. Se calcula el vector en pantalla desde la posición previa del tren (o posición actual si está arrancando) hacia la próxima estación ($S_{next}$).
2. Se calcula el ángulo matemático en grados usando arcotangente 2 (`Math.atan2`):
   $$\theta = \text{atan2}(\Delta Y_{svg}, \Delta X_{svg}) \times \frac{180}{\pi}$$
3. Este ángulo se inyecta en una etiqueta SVG de rotación `<g transform="rotate(theta)">`.
4. El marcador del tren dibuja una **punta/nariz triangular** fuera del círculo y un **chevron de dirección interno** orientados exactamente a lo largo de las vías en la dirección de la marcha.

title: B. Sistema de Seguimiento y Foco (Pinning Mode)
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 5. Sistema de Seguimiento Direccional y Pineo > B. Sistema de Seguimiento y Foco (Pinning Mode)
Al hacer clic en un tren y seleccionar **"Seguir Formación"**:
1. Se guarda el ID del tren en el estado `pinnedTrainId`. 2. El cálculo de los límites del mapa (`finalMinLat`, `finalMaxLat`, etc.) se reajusta para encerrar un cuadrante de tamaño fijo (zoom de ~1.3km) centrado exactamente en la posición del tren. 3. Cada vez que llega un reporte de telemetría (cada 10 segundos) y el tren se mueve, el mapa se desplaza automáticamente manteniéndolo en el centro absoluto (`500, 360` del SVG). 4. El tren seguido se destaca visualmente con un **anillo de tracking rotativo segmentado** (`strokeDasharray` animado) para denotar que el rastreo GPS está activo. 5.

title: B. Sistema de Seguimiento y Foco (Pinning Mode)
text:
Guía Técnica y Arquitectura de `subte-monitor` > 5. Sistema de Seguimiento Direccional y Pineo > B. Sistema de Seguimiento y Foco (Pinning Mode)

title: Guide 01: General Architecture Overview
text:
Guide 01: General Architecture Overview
This document explains the general architecture of the `subte-monitor` application. It details how data flows through our system, how the server communicates with the Buenos Aires City Government's Transit API, and how that information reaches the client browser.

---

1. High-Level Data Flow
The flow of data in the system moves through four major stages:

title: A. Raw Data Retrieval (Server Side)
text:
Guide 01: General Architecture Overview > 1. High-Level Data Flow > A. Raw Data Retrieval (Server Side)
Every time a client makes a request to our telemetry endpoint, or every few seconds, our Next.js backend server makes a request to the Government of Buenos Aires Transit API (GCBA API).
*   **Source URL**: `https://apitransporte.buenosaires.gob.ar/subtes/forecastGTFS`
*   **Format**: The data is fetched in GTFS Realtime JSON format.
*   **Content**: This feed provides real-time arrival estimates (predictions) for each line, stop, and direction. For instance, "Train on Line D is expected to arrive at station Agüero in 180 seconds."

title: B. Core Telemetry Processing (Server Side)
text:
Guide 01: General Architecture Overview > 1. High-Level Data Flow > B. Core Telemetry Processing (Server Side)
Because the raw GCBA API does not provide persistent identifiers for physical trains, our server processes this arrival data in real-time before returning it.
*   **Location**: `src/lib/telemetry.ts`
*   **Actions**:
    1.  **Clustering**: Groups various station predictions together to detect distinct physical trains (using the 1D Clustering Algorithm).
    2.  **Stable Hashing**: Assigns stable IDs like `D-8B4A` so a train keeps the same name throughout its run.
    3.  **Holding at the Signal**: Determines whether a train is at a platform (`STOPPED`) or moving (`IN_TRANSIT`), and prevents it from jumping ahead if the API lags.

title: C. Live API Endpoint (Next.js App Route)
text:
Guide 01: General Architecture Overview > 1. High-Level Data Flow > C. Live API Endpoint (Next.js App Route)
The processed telemetry data is exposed through a Next.js dynamic App Route.
*   **Route Path**: `/api/telemetry`
*   **Location**: `src/app/api/telemetry/route.ts`
*   **Caches**: Implements a short-lived cache of 1.5 seconds to limit outbound API calls and avoid getting rate-limited by GCBA.

D. Client-Side Rendering (Browser Side)
The user interface displays this processed telemetry on an interactive map and boarding screens.
*   **Entry Point**: `src/components/SubteDashboard.tsx`
*   **Actions**:
    1.  **Polling**: Fetches `/api/telemetry` every 2 seconds.
    2.  **Map rendering**: Visualizes train markers moving along lines using Leaflet.
    3.  **UI Updates**: Shows boarding departure lists, connection panels, and live arrivals.

---

title: 2. Full Data Lifecycle Breakdown
text:
Guide 01: General Architecture Overview > 2. Full Data Lifecycle Breakdown
```text
[GCBA Transit API]
       │
       ▼ (Fetch raw GTFS Realtime Forecast / Service Alerts)
[Next.js Backend Server]
       │
       ├─► [Read static database shapes and station IDs via Prisma]
       ├─► [Process with Track-Slot Clustering & Stable ID Hashing]
       ▼
[Next.js REST API Endpoint: /api/telemetry]
       │
       ▼ (Client pulls data every 2000ms using fetch requests)
[Browser UI: SubteDashboard React Component]
       │
       ├─► [Update Leaflet Map Layers with new marker coordinates]
       └─► [Refresh Live Arrival Lists in Station Details Panel]
```

---

title: 3. Tech Stack and Code Responsibilities
text:
Guide 01: General Architecture Overview > 3. Tech Stack and Code Responsibilities
*   **Next.js 15+ (App Router)**: Serves as our web application framework. It renders components on the server for initial speed (SSR) and handles server-side API routing.
*   **TypeScript**: Provides type safety across our application, helping to catch code typos and parameter mismatches before compilation.
*   **Prisma ORM**: A database client that lets us interact with our PostgreSQL database using simple TypeScript methods instead of writing raw SQL.
*   **Leaflet Map**: A lightweight JavaScript library used to render the full-screen interactive train map on the frontend.
*   **Tailwind CSS**: A utility-first CSS framework used to build our clean, glassmorphic dark-mode design system.

title: Guide 03: Database Models & Schema Guide
text:
Guide 03: Database Models & Schema Guide
This document explains the data models of our application, how the database schema is defined using Prisma ORM, how to apply changes, and how the network details are initialized.

---

1. Database Schema File Overview
Our database is managed using Prisma. The definitions of all database tables (models) are saved inside the file:
`prisma/schema.prisma`

title: A. Station Model (Station)
text:
Guide 03: Database Models & Schema Guide > 1. Database Schema File Overview > Model Descriptions > A. Station Model (Station)
Stores the physical locations of stations.
*   `stopId` (String, Primary Key): Unique GTFS ID representing the station platform (e.g. `9 de Julio` platform has one ID for north and one for south).
*   `stopName` (String): The human-readable name of the station (e.g. "Congreso de Tucumán").
*   `latitude` (Float) & `longitude` (Float): Spatial coordinates of the station.

title: B. RouteSequence Model (RouteSequence)
text:
Guide 03: Database Models & Schema Guide > 1. Database Schema File Overview > Model Descriptions > B. RouteSequence Model (RouteSequence)
Maps stations to their corresponding line and ordering.
*   `routeId` (String): Identifies the line (e.g. `LineaD`, `PM-Civico`).
*   `directionId` (Int): 0 for outbound trips, 1 for return trips.
*   `stopSequence` (Int): The physical order number of the station on the track (from 1 to N).
*   `stopId` (String): Reference to the physical `Station`.

title: C. Report Model (Report)
text:
Guide 03: Database Models & Schema Guide > 1. Database Schema File Overview > Model Descriptions > C. Report Model (Report)
Stores user-reported incidents (delay notifications, escalator breakdowns, etc.).
*   `line` (String): The route affected.
*   `station` (String): Normalized station name where the issue occurred.
*   `category` (String): The problem type (e.g., "Demora", "Frecuencia").
*   `comment` (String): User's description.
*   `createdAt` (DateTime): Automated timestamp.

---

title: 2. Common Database Tasks & Commands
text:
Guide 03: Database Models & Schema Guide > 2. Common Database Tasks & Commands
To modify database structures, run the following commands in your terminal:

A. How to Update the Database Schema
1.  Open `prisma/schema.prisma`.
2.  Modify or add fields. For example, to add an `email` field to the `Report` model:
    ```prisma
    model Report {
      ...
      userEmail String?
    }
    ```
3.  Save the file.
4.  Run `npx prisma db push` to synchronize your local database structure with the schema.
5.  Run `npx prisma generate` to rebuild the TypeScript client libraries so your code recognizes the new fields.

title: B. Seeding the Database
text:
Guide 03: Database Models & Schema Guide > 2. Common Database Tasks & Commands > B. Seeding the Database
The project contains static GTFS station coordinates and sequence routes. To populate the database with these default records:
1.  Run the command:
    ```bash
    npx prisma db seed
    ```
    This script executes `prisma/seed.ts`, parses the GTFS coordinates, and uploads them to your database.

---

title: 3. Database Safety Guards (CRITICAL)
text:
Guide 03: Database Models & Schema Guide > 3. Database Safety Guards (CRITICAL)
To prevent developer errors from wiping production database sales data (such as accidentally pointing migrations to Kermingo's database), a database shield configuration is enabled:
*   **Protection File**: `prisma.config.ts`
*   **Action**: Halts execution immediately if the environment variable `DATABASE_URL` contains the substring `kermingo`.
*   **Rules**: Never edit, remove, or bypass this configuration.

title: Guide 04: Telemetry & Stateful Tracking Engine
text:
Guide 04: Telemetry & Stateful Tracking Engine
This document outlines the telemetry processing algorithms inside `src/lib/telemetry.ts` that convert plain station arrivals into a real-time tracking visualization.

---

1. The Challenge of Tracking Without Train IDs
The Buenos Aires Transit API (GCBA API) does not tell us: "Train A is currently at coordinates X, Y". Instead, it sends an array of estimated arrivals:
*   "Train will arrive at Station 1 in 60 seconds."
*   "Train will arrive at Station 2 in 180 seconds."

To reconstruct the actual physical trains, the engine performs the following processing sequence every time `/api/telemetry` is called.

---

title: A. DBSCAN 1D (Spatial-Temporal Clustering)
text:
Guide 04: Telemetry & Stateful Tracking Engine > 2. Core Tracking Algorithms > A. DBSCAN 1D (Spatial-Temporal Clustering)
1.  For every arrival estimate, we calculate its projected starting time from the terminal:
    $$\text{Start Time} = \text{Arrival Time} - (\text{Stop Sequence} \times 88.5\text{ seconds})$$
    where $88.5$ seconds is the average travel time between adjacent stations.
2.  If multiple station predictions point to the same projected start time (within a **180-second** window), they are grouped together.
3.  Each cluster represents **one physical train** currently traveling on the tracks.

title: B. Stable ID Hashing
text:
Guide 04: Telemetry & Stateful Tracking Engine > 2. Core Tracking Algorithms > B. Stable ID Hashing
To assign a permanent ID to a train without maintaining complex database sessions:
1.  We calculate the average projected start time for the cluster.
2.  We round this time into slots of **150 seconds** to tolerate slight prediction fluctuations.
3.  We generate an MD5 hash using the line, direction, and rounded time slot:
    $$\text{Hash} = \text{MD5}(\text{routeId} + \text{directionId} + \text{roundedStart})$$
    We take the first 4 characters of this hash to create a stable ID like `D-A4FC`.

title: C. Holding at the Signal (Anti-Teleportation)
text:
Guide 04: Telemetry & Stateful Tracking Engine > 2. Core Tracking Algorithms > C. Holding at the Signal (Anti-Teleportation)
To prevent trains from "jumping" positions when the API updates slowly:
1.  We measure `etaEnPaquete` (the arrival estimate relative to the API's own feed timestamp).
2.  A train is only marked as `STOPPED` at a station when `etaEnPaquete` is $\le 15$ seconds.
3.  While `IN_TRANSIT`, progress is calculated locally using the server time:
    $$\text{Progress} = \text{Math.max}\left(0.0, \text{Math.min}\left(0.95, 1 - \frac{\text{secondsToArrival}}{90}\right)\right)$$
    Note the ceiling at **0.95 (95%)**. If local time keeps ticking but the API feed does not update to confirm the train has arrived, the train remains held at 95% of the track instead of jumping to the next station.

title: D. Dead Reckoning
text:
Guide 04: Telemetry & Stateful Tracking Engine > 2. Core Tracking Algorithms > D. Dead Reckoning
If a train disappears from the API feed for a short period (up to 40 seconds), the engine continues to project its location using its last known velocity rather than letting it vanish instantly. If the API returns completely empty (no service or nighttime closure), the cache is cleared (`trackerDB.clear()`), and all trains are removed immediately.

---

title: 3. Server Cache Configuration
text:
Guide 04: Telemetry & Stateful Tracking Engine > 3. Server Cache Configuration
The telemetry server cache prevents overloading the external transit API:
*   **Cache Limit**: 1.5 seconds.
*   **Behavior**: If multiple users request map updates within 1.5 seconds, they all receive the same cached data, reducing server load.

title: Guide 05: Frontend Leaflet Map & UI Guide
text:
Guide 05: Frontend Leaflet Map & UI Guide
This document explains the frontend architecture of our application, specifically focusing on the Leaflet Map integration, screen layouts, responsive mobile controls, and transfer (connections) logic.

---

1. File Location & Layout Structure
The entire frontend user interface is contained inside:
`src/components/SubteDashboard.tsx`

title: Screen Navigation (Tabs)
text:
Guide 05: Frontend Leaflet Map & UI Guide > 1. File Location & Layout Structure > Screen Navigation (Tabs)
The dashboard uses a state variable called `currentTab` to control which screen is active.
*   `'map'`: Shows the full-screen interactive Leaflet map with live train positions.
*   `'planner'`: Pathfinding routing screen using Dijkstra's algorithm.
*   `'stations'`: Station list directory with live arrival logs and accessibility details.
*   `'status'`: Service alerts, delays, and historical passenger statistics.
*   `'arrivals'`: Boarding timetables grouped by line and direction.

---

title: A. Dark Mode Street Layout
B. Track and Train Markers Rendering
text:
Guide 05: Frontend Leaflet Map & UI Guide > 2. Interactive Leaflet Map Configuration > B. Track and Train Markers Rendering
1.  **Station Circles**: Station stops are plotted on the map using coordinates from our database.
2.  **Track Shapes**: Track lines are drawn on the map using static GTFS track shape segments imported from `src/lib/shapes.ts`.
3.  **Train Markers**: Train icons are customized HTML divs (`L.divIcon`) containing:
    *   A colored circle matching the route color.
    *   A tiny arrow indicating train heading direction.
    *   An ID label displaying the train hash (e.g. `B-4F8A`).

---

title: 3. Responsive Mobile Line Selector
text:
Guide 05: Frontend Leaflet Map & UI Guide > 3. Responsive Mobile Line Selector
*   **Location**: Rendered as a floating horizontal selector at the top of the map view.
*   **Behavior**: Scrollable badge list visible only on mobile screens (`md:hidden`).
*   **Action**: Clicking a badge triggers the `setActiveLine` state, filtering active train markers and zoom bounds for that specific line.

---

title: 4. Transfer and Connection Logic
B. Station Directory Combination Badges
text:
Guide 05: Frontend Leaflet Map & UI Guide > 4. Transfer and Connection Logic > B. Station Directory Combination Badges
In the stations list pane, when you select a station, it queries `initialStations` to locate connected nodes by name or manual walk-tunnels. It shows their line badges but filters them out if they share the selected station's route ID, ensuring that only cross-line connections are shown.

title: Guide 06: Running, Deployment, & Production Operations
text:
Guide 06: Running, Deployment, & Production Operations
This document lists the step-by-step commands to configure, test, run, and deploy the `subte-monitor` project.

---

1. Local Configuration Check
Before running the application, make sure you have created your configuration files in the root folder:

A. Environment Configuration File (`.env`)
Create a file named `.env` in the root folder and add the following keys:
```env
# Database Connection URL (PostgreSQL)
DATABASE_URL="postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/subtemonitor"

# Buenos Aires City Transit Credentials (Optional - Defaults are used if empty)
SUBTE_CLIENT_ID="your_client_id"
SUBTE_CLIENT_SECRET="your_client_secret"
```

---

title: 2. Command Reference Checklist
text:
Guide 06: Running, Deployment, & Production Operations > 2. Command Reference Checklist
Execute these commands inside your project root folder:

A. Install Project Dependencies
Run this command once before running the app to fetch all package requirements:
```bash
npm install
```

B. Run the Local Development Server
Starts the application in development mode with hot reloading:
```bash
npm run dev
```
Open your browser at `http://localhost:3000` to preview the project.

title: C. Build the Project for Production
text:
Guide 06: Running, Deployment, & Production Operations > 2. Command Reference Checklist > C. Build the Project for Production
Compiles and type-checks the source files, producing an optimized build folder:
```bash
npm run build
```

D. Sync Schema to Database
Pushes model changes from `prisma/schema.prisma` directly to your database:
```bash
npx prisma db push
```

E. Run the Database Seed Script
Populates the database with static GTFS network coordinates:
```bash
npx prisma db seed
```

---

title: 3. Production Deployment (Vercel)
text:
Guide 06: Running, Deployment, & Production Operations > 3. Production Deployment (Vercel)
The application is deployed on Vercel. To deploy changes manually:

1.  Log in to Vercel via CLI if you haven't already:
    ```bash
    npx vercel login
    ```
2.  Run the production deployment command:
    ```bash
    npx vercel --prod --yes
    ```
    This uploads the code, builds it on the cloud, and updates the production URL:
    `https://subte-monitor.vercel.app`

title: Anden, the AI layer
text:
Anden, the AI layer
Anden adds an assistant layer on top of `subte-monitor` in five stages: an MCP server, retrieval, memory, evals, and a harness. Each stage is additive and runs without a database. This page records what is built and how to check it.

Stage 1: subte-mcp
`packages/subte-mcp` is a standalone npm package that publishes the live subway data as MCP tools over stdio. It imports nothing from the Next app and uses no database or Prisma. Its only runtime dependencies are `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` and `zod`.

It reads two public endpoints on the deployed app:

| Endpoint | Used for | Caching |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/api/bootstrap` | Stations and GTFS stop sequences | 10 minutes, in memory |
| `/api/telemetry` | Trains, alerts, predictions | Never cached |

title: Anden, the AI layer
text:
Anden, the AI layer
The base URL comes from `SUBTE_API_BASE` and defaults to the live deployment. Requests time out after 5 seconds and retry once on a network failure. A 4xx response is not retried.

title: Tools
text:
Anden, the AI layer > Stage 1: subte-mcp > Tools
| Tool | Arguments | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `subway_status` | `line?` | Alerts grouped by line, `stale`, feed age |
| `next_trains` | `station`, `line?`, `limit=3` | Arrivals at one station sorted by ETA |
| `plan_trip` | `from`, `to`, `step_free=false` | Legs, transfers, stop count, minutes |
| `nearby_stations` | `lat`, `lng`, `radius_m=800` | Stations with distance in meters |

Station names match without case or accents, so `Agüero`, `aguero`, and `AGUERO` reach the same station. A name that matches several stations returns the candidates instead of a guess.

title: Tools
text:
Anden, the AI layer > Stage 1: subte-mcp > Tools
The planner runs Dijkstra over two kinds of edge: a ride between adjacent stops costs 2 minutes, a transfer costs 3. Transfers come from stations with the same name on different lines plus the interchange pairs in `packages/subte-mcp/src/data/transfers.json`. The app's `STATION_CONNECTIONS` map in `src/lib/connections.ts` only lists bus and rail links, so the package keeps its own list of underground interchanges. Floor access comes from `packages/subte-mcp/src/data/accessibility.json`, copied from `ACCESSIBILITY_METADATA` in `src/lib/metadata.ts`. With `step_free=true`, transfers at stations without an elevator are removed.

Client setup, request and response examples, and the limits live in [packages/subte-mcp/README.md](../packages/subte-mcp/README.md).

title: Build and check
text:
Anden, the AI layer > Stage 1: subte-mcp > Build and check
Run from the repository root:

```bash
npm --prefix packages/subte-mcp run build
node packages/subte-mcp/test/smoke.mjs
npx tsc --noEmit
```

The smoke test spawns the built server with the SDK client against the live API. It does not need a key. Last run:

```text
tools/list ok: nearby_stations, next_trains, plan_trip, subway_status
subway_status ok: stale=false feedAge=2s alerts=3
subway_status filter ok: ["LineaB"]
next_trains ok: 2 arrivals at Uruguay
next_trains accent/case match ok
plan_trip ok: 7 stops, 1 transfers, 17 min
plan_trip step-free ok: 7 stops, 1 transfers
nearby_stations ok: 11 stations within 800m
error mapping ok: unknown station
error mapping ok: ambiguous station
error mapping ok: same station
error mapping ok: unknown line
smoke test passed against https://subte-monitor.vercel.app
```

title: Build and check
text:
Anden, the AI layer > Stage 1: subte-mcp > Build and check
Warm medians from a local run, Node 22.23, against the live API:

| Tool | Median call | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `subway_status` | 415 ms | 0.9 KB |
| `next_trains` | 413 ms | 0.4 KB |
| `plan_trip` | 6 ms | 0.4 KB |
| `nearby_stations` | 2 ms | 1.3 KB |

title: Limits
text:
Anden, the AI layer > Stage 1: subte-mcp > Limits
- Linea D is simulated by the app instead of coming from the GCBA feed. The server passes through what `/api/telemetry` reports, so D arrivals appear when the simulated feed has them. When a D-only station has no arrivals, the response carries a note saying so.
- Trip durations are estimates from the 2 minute and 3 minute assumptions and exclude the first wait. Use `next_trains` for the real ETA.
- The reference feed is mostly unaccented. Matching removes accents, but a misspelling more than two edits away falls back to a closest-name error.
- Stations missing from the accessibility data count as not step-free, so some step-free trips report no route.
